3: Hypothesis refinement: turn a hunch into something data can say yes or no to. Four stages. One, vague: page value matters. Two, specific: sessions that saw a valued page buy more often. Three, testable: compare the buy rate where page values is above zero versus equal to zero. Four, a decision rule: chi square p value below point oh five means keep the idea. The rule: write the hypothesis and the decision rule before you look at the result.
4: Two hypotheses, tested. Hypothesis one: a valued page leads to more buying. With page values equal to zero, the buy rate is three point nine percent, and with page values above zero, fifty six point three percent. The p value is about zero, so keep. Hypothesis two: new visitors buy more. New visitors buy at twenty four point nine percent, other visitors nineteen point eight, and returning visitors fourteen point one, with a p value of four times ten to the minus twenty nine. Keep. Both pass the rule. Hypothesis one is huge: a session that saw a valued page is fourteen times more likely to buy.
5: Train test logic is like practice questions versus the final exam. The model studies the training rows, which is practice. The test rows are the exam, locked away and used once, at the end. Here there are nine thousand seven hundred sixty four training rows, eighty percent, and two thousand four hundred forty one test rows, twenty percent. Stratify so both parts keep the same share of buyers, fifteen point six percent in train and in test. Fix random state so anyone gets the same split. 6: Five fold cross validation: five mini exams inside the training rows. The training data is split into five folds. Each fold in turn is used to check while the other four are used to learn. The five R O C A U C scores are point eight nine three, point nine oh two, point eight eight, point eight eight seven and point eight eight nine. The mean is point eight nine, with a spread, standard deviation, of plus or minus point oh oh seven. A small spread means stable. Why: one split can be lucky, five give a mean and a spread. And the test set is still untouched.
7: Data leakage: the model sees information it will not have when used for real. Four kinds. Target leakage: a feature created after the outcome, like payment confirmed to predict buying. Train test contamination: the same row in both parts, for example duplicates, and we had one hundred twenty five. Preprocessing leakage: a scaler, imputer or feature selection fitted on all rows before the split. Sampling leakage: over sampling before the split, so copies of a row land in both train and test. The result: great scores in the notebook, poor results in real life.
8: Leakage on real data: the same model, in two orders. If you over sample then split, the recall is point nine nine two, and ninety eight point four percent of the test buyers had an exact copy in train. That is the leaky version. If you split first and then over sample only the training rows, the recall is point six six five. That is the honest version. Why: the leaky model was tested on rows it had already memorised. The lesson: the honest point six six five is lower, and it is the number you can trust.
9: Preventing data leakage. Remove duplicates first. Split first, before any fitting or resampling. Fit every step on training rows only. Resample, over or under, the training rows only. Ask of every feature: is it known at prediction time? And use the test set once. A pipeline helps: make pipeline with standard scaler then logistic regression. A pipeline re fits the scaler inside each cross validation fold, so there is no peeking.
10: Lecture thirty: skewed data and insights. Only fifteen point six percent of sessions end in a purchase.
11: The accuracy paradox. A model that always says no buy has an accuracy of eighty four point four percent, but finds zero percent of buyers, a recall of zero. With a skewed target, accuracy mostly measures the big class. So report recall, which is buyers found, F one and R O C A U C. And always compare with the always no baseline.
12: Sampling skewed data. Taking a small sample for a quick look: a two percent sample is two hundred forty four rows. A random sample has eighteen percent buyers, against the true fifteen point six. A stratified sample has exactly fifteen point six percent. Stratified means sampling the same fraction from each class, so the mix stays true. The code is df group by Revenue, sample with frac equal to point oh two. The same idea, stratify equals y in train test split, keeps fifteen point six percent buyers in both parts.
13: Three ways to handle skew in training. No change: accuracy point eight eight nine, recall point four one six, F one point five four one. Class weight balanced: accuracy point eight five one, recall point seven eight five, F one point six two three. Under sampling: point eight four seven, point seven eight five, point six one seven. Over sampling: point eight four eight, point seven nine one, point six two. A small drop in accuracy, but recall nearly doubles. Class weight balanced needs no extra rows. And do all of this on training rows only, because resampling before the split is the leak from lecture twenty nine.
14: Translating E D A into insights: observation, evidence, meaning, action. Valued pages drive buying: fifty six point three percent versus three point nine percent buy, which means intent shows on product pages, so push visitors to product pages. November is the peak: November twenty five point five percent, October twenty point nine, which means holiday shopping, so plan stock and ads for the fourth quarter. New visitors buy more: twenty four point nine versus fourteen point one percent, which means first visits are purposeful, so offer a welcome offer for new visitors. The test: a manager can act on it without reading your code.

16: Key takeaways. Refine hypotheses and set the decision rule first. Split first, cross validate on train, and test once. Leakage makes scores lie: point nine nine two versus an honest point six six five. For skewed data, judge by recall and F one, and resample the training rows only. And an insight is observation, evidence, meaning, action.
